opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really interesting question, and it's one where I think people's intuitions often get pulled in a misleading direction by the chimp-to-human comparison itself.

If you look at the biological story, there's a pretty dramatic discontinuity in impact. Chimps and humans are not that different in brain size or architecture, maybe a factor of three in brain size and some changes, and yet humans went on to transform the planet while chimps didn't. So it's tempting to say a small change in intelligence produced an enormous change in outcomes, and therefore we should expect AI to have a similarly sharp threshold where it goes from not very useful to transformative.

But I think a lot of that discontinuity comes from the specifics of evolution rather than from the nature of intelligence. Evolution wasn't optimizing chimps to be good at, say, accumulating culture or doing science. It was optimizing for reproductive fitness in a particular niche. Humans crossed some threshold where cultural accumulation took off: language, teaching, building on what previous generations figured out. Once that happened, you get this huge compounding effect that's driven by culture over tens of thousands of years, not really by individual brains getting smarter. So the abruptness is about a new feedback loop switching on, in a process that wasn't aiming for it.

With AI the situation is pretty different. We're deliberately optimizing systems to be economically useful, and people are paying close attention to how useful they are at every stage. If there were some cheap change that made a system dramatically more valuable, there's a lot of pressure to find it early. So my default expectation is that you see value ramp up more continuously. You'd have AI systems that are somewhat useful, then quite useful, then automating large fractions of tasks, before you get systems that are as good as humans at everything. There's a "chimp-level" AI that's still worth a lot of money because it's doing things we specifically trained it to do.

That said, I don't think "continuous" means "slow." I'd expect the overall transition to be quite fast by historical standards. Once you have AI substantially accelerating AI research and the economy more broadly, you can get growth rates that look wild compared to anything we've seen, maybe the economy doubling in a year or less, rather than every couple of decades. So the picture I have is something like: a smooth-ish curve, but a curve that gets very steep. You'd see it coming in the sense that there would be a few years where AI is obviously having a huge and growing economic impact before things go completely crazy.

Where I'd put meaningful probability on something more abrupt is if there's some ingredient, analogous to cultural learning, that current systems are missing and that unlocks a lot at once. I don't think that's crazy. I just don't think the chimp-human analogy is strong evidence for it, because the reason evolution produced a jump is mostly that it wasn't looking for the thing that mattered, and we are.

r001.rationale: The response says chimp-level AI could be valuable when trained for specific tasks, but it does not claim that fully domesticated chimps would provide substantial economic value.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the chimps-to-humans analogy is one people reach for a lot, and I'm pretty skeptical that it tells you much about abruptness in the AI case. The reason is that the thing that happened between chimps and humans wasn't really a thing that happened on the axis of economic value at all. Evolution wasn't optimizing for economic output. It was optimizing for fitness, and that's just a very different objective, so the fact that a small change in brain size or whatever produced a huge jump in what you could do with the resulting creatures doesn't tell you that a small change in the relevant inputs to an AI system would produce a similarly huge jump.

If you ask the question the way I'd actually want to ask it, which is something like, suppose you held fixed the amount of effort going into making these systems smarter and you watched economic value as a function of that effort, then I think the chimp-human comparison is mostly uninformative. Chimps were never being selected for being economically useful to humans. We don't have the data point of a chimp that's been trained really hard on tasks and then a slightly smarter chimp trained really hard, and seeing how the value jumps. What we observe is one species that wasn't being optimized for this at all and then another species that, over a very long time, built up a lot of culture and institutions and so on that make it productive.

And I think that last part is actually the key thing. A huge fraction of what makes humans economically valuable isn't raw individual intelligence, it's the accumulated stuff, the language, the tools, the ability to pass knowledge forward. A single human raised in isolation is not that impressive relative to a chimp. So even on the biological side, the apparent discontinuity is kind of a trick. You see a big gap in outcomes and attribute it to the intelligence difference, when a lot of it is this slow compounding process that got unlocked.

So my overall view is that when you're actually scaling up AI systems, you're doing the thing that evolution wasn't doing. You're directly pushing on the economically relevant capabilities, and you're deploying each version into the world as you go. In that regime I expect the increase to be pretty continuous. Not slow necessarily, it could be fast in calendar time, but continuous in the sense that each generation of system is somewhat more useful than the last and you're getting a lot of value out of the intermediate ones. If I had to put numbers on it I'd say something like, I expect economic impact to be growing smoothly and I'd be surprised, though not shocked, to see a single jump where you go from systems that are basically useless to systems that are transformative without passing through a bunch of pretty useful intermediate systems.

The place where I'd be most worried about abruptness is less about the intelligence scaling itself and more about things like, do you cross some threshold where the systems can do AI research and that kicks off a feedback loop. That's a real mechanism for discontinuity, but it's a different argument than the chimp one, and I think it's worth keeping them separate.

r001.rationale: The response does not claim that fully domesticated chimps would provide substantial economic value. It says chimps were not selected for economic usefulness and offers no such domestication claim.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you’re holding fixed. If you imagine taking a chimp and gradually making it smarter, then asking how much someone would pay to employ it, you could see a pretty sharp increase. There are lots of tasks where being almost able to do the task isn’t worth very much, and being able to do it reliably is worth a lot.

But I don’t think that necessarily means there’s some very sharp underlying discontinuity in intelligence. You could have a smooth improvement in capability that crosses the threshold where it becomes economically useful.

And humans are a somewhat tricky comparison because so much of our productivity comes from culture. A human raised without access to human knowledge and institutions is much less economically productive than a person who can learn from everyone else. So part of the question is: when does your smarter chimp become able to participate in that process? If it can learn language, follow instructions, and pick up skills from humans, its value could rise quite quickly. But the chimp-to-human comparison alone doesn’t tell us how narrow that transition is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a chimp gradually becoming smarter and potentially gaining value once it can perform tasks, but it does not claim that fully domesticated chimps would already provide substantial economic value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you’re holding fixed. If you imagine taking a chimp and making it a little smarter, while leaving the rest of the world unchanged, you might get very little economic value for a while. Then, as it becomes able to understand instructions and do jobs that humans want done, its value could rise pretty quickly.

But that’s different from asking how much economic output a whole civilization of those creatures could produce. Humans benefit enormously from language, accumulated knowledge, and all the institutions and technology we’ve built. You don’t get those just by turning up the intelligence of one individual.

So I’d expect there to be a range where relatively small improvements in intelligence lead to very large improvements in economic usefulness. I’m less convinced that there’s some single sharp threshold between chimp and human where everything suddenly happens. And the chimp-to-human comparison by itself doesn’t tell us how narrow that range is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says economic value might remain low until chimps can understand instructions and do desired jobs. It does not claim that fully domesticated chimps would already provide substantial economic value.
